title: The Mermin-Peres Magic Square Game With Three or More Players
abstract: We present a generalization of the Mermin-Peres magic square game to $N$ players, in which the square is replaced by an $N$-dimensional hypercube. We show that the winning probability of the optimal classical strategy remains $8/9$ for all $N$, while for $N \ge 3$, a generalization of the quantum strategy for $N = 2$ achieves a winning probability between $1/3$ and $3/4$. This loss of quantum advantage for $N \ge 3$ is a consequence of monogamy.
summary: This work generalizes the Mermin-Peres magic square game to N players on an N-dimensional hypercube. It rigorously proves that while the optimal classical strategy yields a winning probability of 8/9 for any N, the quantum advantage vanishes for N >= 3. This loss of advantage is theoretically linked to the principle of monogamy of entanglement.
main_problem: The paper generalizes the Mermin-Peres magic square game to N players using an N-dimensional hypercube to compare classical and quantum winning probabilities.
main_result: For N >= 3, the quantum winning probability is bounded between 1/3 and 3/4, which is strictly less than the classical winning probability of 8/9, demonstrating a loss of quantum advantage due to monogamy.
method: The analysis involves constructing the game on an N-dimensional hypercube and using techniques from quantum information theory, specifically analyzing the constraints imposed by anti-commuting Pauli operators.
model_or_system: The model is the Mermin-Peres magic square game generalized to N players, involving measurements on qubits across an N-dimensional hypercube structure.
key_observables: Winning probability (Prob(Win)) and the probability of consensus among players.
important_parameters: The number of players, N (especially N >= 3), and the structure of the hypercube.
main_assumptions: The analysis is restricted to Pauli measurements on qubits and assumes a specific generalization of the game rules.

paper_structure: The paper first reviews the classical strategy, establishing the 8/9 bound. It then generalizes the quantum strategy, deriving upper bounds ($\le 3/4$) and lower bounds ($\ge 1/3$) for $N \ge 3$ by analyzing constraints from anti-commuting observables, concluding with the implication of monogamy.
why_interesting: It provides a concrete, non-trivial example where quantum correlations fail to provide an advantage over classical strategies, offering insights into the limitations imposed by entanglement structure (monogamy).
